claim: The corn snake HoxD cluster is about 1.5 fold larger than the mouse HoxD cluster.
source: When compared to the mouse, the corn snake cluster is about 1.5 fold larger (Figure 1A) (Vonk et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison data presented in the manuscript and cited literature (Vonk et al., 2013).

claim: All Hoxd genes except Hoxd12 are present in the corn snake HoxD cluster.
source: The structural analysis of the corn snake HoxD cluster revealed that, as for other species of snakes whose genomes were recently released (Vonk et al., 2013; Castoe et al., 2013), all Hoxd genes but Hoxd12 are present and share the same transcriptional orientation within the cluster.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of the sequenced corn snake HoxD cluster and comparison with other snake genomes.

claim: The corn snake HoxD cluster contains more than twice as many repeats as the mouse counterpart.
source: We found that the corn snake cluster contains more than twice as many repeats as the mouse counterpart.
evidence: The claim is supported by repeat content analysis performed on the sequenced genomes.

claim: The mouse HoxD cluster is mainly composed of SINEs while the corn snake cluster is composed of different types of transposable elements including LINEs and DNA transposons.
source: In addition, while the mouse HoxD cluster is mainly composed of SINEs (short interspersed elements), the corn snake cluster is composed of different types of transposable elements including LINEs (long interspersed elements) and DNA transposons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by repeat element analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No particular H3K9me3 enrichment was scored over the length of the snake HoxD cluster.
source: No particular H3K9me3 enrichment was scored over the length of the HoxD cluster and the closest located peak was identified in an intron of the Lunapark gene, i.e. at a position unlikely to have any critical impact on Hoxd gene expression (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq experimental data for H3K9me3 in snake embryonic brain tissue.

claim: The entire snake HoxD cluster was decorated with H3K27me3 marks in embryonic brain tissue where Hox genes are not expressed.
source: In the absence of Hox gene transcription (brain), the entire cluster was decorated with H3K27me3 marks, forming a dense domain of Polycomb repression as seen previously in other species.
evidence: The claim is supported by H3K27me3 ChIP-seq data in snake brain tissue.

claim: The posterior trunk tissue of snake embryos displayed H3K27me3 coverage specifically over the 5' part of the gene cluster containing the most 'posterior' Hoxd genes.
source: In contrast, the posterior trunk tissue displayed an H3K27me3 coverage specifically over the 5' part of the gene cluster, containing the most 'posterior' Hoxd genes (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on H3K27me3 ChIP-seq data from snake posterior trunk tissue.

claim: There is a clear correlation between the domain of active Hoxd genes and the absence of the H3K27me3 mark in snake embryos.
source: In parallel, whole-mount in situ hybridization (WISH) to assess Hoxd gene expression revealed a clear correlation between the domain of active Hoxd genes and the absence of the H3K27me3 mark (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by combined WISH and ChIP-seq data.

claim: Both spatial collinearity and the associated dynamics of chromatin structure accompanying progressive gene activation are implemented in snakes as in any other vertebrate species studied thus far.
source: From these experiments, we concluded that both spatial collinearity and the associated dynamics of chromatin structure accompanying progressive gene activation are implemented in snakes as in any other vertebrate species studied thus far.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the chromatin modification and gene expression data presented.

claim: All mammalian transgenic BACs showed Hoxd4 transcript patterns restricted to the dorsal part of the main embryonic body axis.
source: The expression of Hoxd4 was monitored by in situ hybridization with species-specific probes and, under these experimental conditions, all mammalian transgenic BACs showed transcript patterns restricted to the dorsal part of the main embryonic body axis (Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization experiments with BAC transgenic mice.

claim: The human Hoxd4 gene was expressed only in the neural tube at the stage examined.
source: We found that, at least at this stage of development, the human Hoxd4 gene was expressed only in the neural tube (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on WISH analysis of sectioned embryos from the human BAC transgenic line.

claim: The chicken and zebrafish BAC transgenic lines showed Hoxd4 expression patterns similar to mammalian BACs, mostly limited to the neural tube and dorsal-most part of the somites.
source: We then investigated the expression of Hoxd4 from either the chicken or the zebrafish BAC transgenic lines and found a similar expression pattern, again mostly limited to the neural tube as well as the dorsal-most part of the somites (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization data from chicken and zebrafish BAC transgenic mice.

claim: Enhancers controlling the robust expression of Hoxd genes in various mesodermal derivatives are, for the most part, located outside of the cluster itself in most vertebrates.
source: Altogether, these results suggested that enhancers controlling the robust expression of Hoxd genes in various mesodermal derivatives are, for the most part, located outside of the cluster itself.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the BAC transgenic expression patterns observed.

claim: Mouse embryos carrying the HoxDDel(Atf2-Nsi) deletion showed a domain of Hoxd4 expression comparable to control embryos.
source: Mutant embryos carrying this HoxDDel(Atf2-Nsi) deletion (Montavon et al., 2011) showed a domain of Hoxd4 expression comparable to control embryos (Figure 2C; Del(Atf2-Nsi).
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization analysis of mutant mouse embryos.

claim: Embryos carrying the HoxDDel(Attp-Sb3) deletion displayed reduced amounts of Hoxd4 mRNA steady state levels in the ventral mesoderm.
source: In contrast, embryos carrying the HoxDDel(Attp-Sb3) deletion of the opposite TAD, located telomeric to the HoxD cluster, which contains various enhancer sequences (Andrey et al., 2013; Delpretti et al., 2012), displayed reduced amounts of mRNA steady state levels in the ventral mesoderm (Figure 2C; Del(Attp-Sb3).
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization data from mutant embryos.

claim: The telomeric gene desert contains most of the enhancers necessary for Hox gene expression in ventral mesoderm.
source: These results indicate that the telomeric gene desert contains most of the enhancers necessary for Hox gene expression in ventral mesoderm.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on deletion mutant analysis.

claim: The expression of Hoxd3 and Hoxd8 was lost in the ventral mesoderm in the absence of the telomeric gene desert.
source: Similar to Hoxd4, the expression of these two other Hoxd genes was lost in the ventral mesoderm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) thus suggesting that the telomeric gene desert contains sequences necessary for the expression of multiple Hoxd genes in the ventral mesoderm of the upper trunk.
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization data for Hoxd3 and Hoxd8 in deletion mutants.

claim: In the snake BAC transgenic line, expression of Hoxd4 in the trunk was not dorsally restricted and was reminiscent of the endogenous mouse Hoxd4 expression.
source: Next, we analysed the transgenic line carrying the snake HoxD cluster and found that, in this case, expression of Hoxd4 in the trunk was not dorsally restricted as observed in all other vertebrate BACs assayed thus far. The expression pattern in the main body axis was in fact reminiscent of the endogenous mouse Hoxd4 expression, with equally strong signals in both the neural tube and mesodermal derivatives (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization data from the snake BAC transgenic mouse line.

claim: Enhancers located within the snake cluster appear sufficient to drive Hoxd gene expression in the ventral mesoderm.
source: Therefore, in contrast to other vertebrate species, enhancers located within the snake cluster appear sufficient to drive Hoxd gene expression in the ventral mesoderm.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the snake BAC transgenic expression pattern.

claim: While 40% of conserved sequences in the telomeric desert were acetylated in the mouse sample, only 22% of them were significantly decorated by H3K27ac in the snake tissue.
source: While 40% of these conserved sequences were acetylated in the mouse sample, only 22% of them were significantly decorated by this chromatin mark in the snake tissue (Figure 2D, right).
evidence: The claim is based on comparative H3K27ac ChIP-seq analysis between mouse and snake.

claim: The enhancers required to control snake Hoxd gene expression in the trunk mesoderm are, at least for the most part, positioned within the cluster rather than in the telomeric gene desert.
source: Overall, these results indicate that the enhancers required to control snake Hoxd gene expression in the trunk mesoderm are, at least for the most part positioned within the cluster rather than in the telomeric gene desert.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on H3K27ac ChIP-seq and BAC transgenic data.

claim: Significant interactions between the snake viewpoints and the centromeric TAD were observed, mostly when the Hoxd13 bait was used and, to a lower extent, with Hoxd11.
source: As observed in the mouse, significant interactions between the snake viewpoints and the centromeric TAD were observed, mostly when the Hoxd13 bait was used and, to a lower extent, with Hoxd11 (Figure 3A,B, compare tracks 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is based on 4C-seq data from snake embryos.

claim: Snake genes located at different relative positions within the HoxD gene cluster show distinct interaction tropisms, similar to mouse.
source: Therefore, as previously reported in the case of mouse tissues and ES cells, genes located at different relative positions within the HoxD gene cluster show distinct interaction tropisms. 5'-located genes such as Hoxd13 interact primarily with the 5'-located gene desert, whereas genes located in a more 3' part of the cluster, such as Hoxd4, interact mostly with the 3'-located gene desert (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is based on 4C-seq data comparing mouse and snake interaction profiles.

claim: In snake embryonic cells, Hoxd9 and to a much lesser extent Hoxd11 displayed an interaction pattern related to that of Hoxd4 with contacts enriched within the sub-TAD 'a'.
source: In snake embryonic cells, however, Hoxd9 and to a much lesser extent Hoxd11, displayed an interaction pattern related to that of Hoxd4 with contacts enriched within the sub-TAD 'a', suggesting the absence of strong regulatory controls located in region 'b' of the snake gene desert (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and D).
evidence: The claim is based on 4C-seq data from snake embryos.

claim: 3'-located genes such as Hoxd4 are expressed in the snake hemipenes.
source: In situ hybridization revealed that 3'-located genes such as Hoxd4 are expressed in the snake HP (Figure 4A, top)
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization data from snake hemipenes.

claim: In the mouse, neither Hoxd3 nor Hoxd4 are transcribed in external genitalia.
source: In situ hybridization revealed that 3'-located genes such as Hoxd4 are expressed in the snake HP (Figure 4A, top), in contrast to the mouse where neither Hoxd3 nor Hoxd4 are transcribed in this structure (Lonfat et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Lonfat et al., 2014).

claim: The human, mouse, chicken and zebrafish Hoxd genes were expressed mostly along the main body axis and transcribed neither in the limbs, nor in the external genitals in BAC transgenic mice.
source: While the human, mouse, chicken and zebrafish Hoxd genes were expressed mostly along the main body axis and transcribed neither in the limbs, nor in the external genitals, in agreement with previous results (see above and (Lonfat and Duboule, 2015) (Figure 4A, bottom and Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization data from BAC transgenic mice.

claim: The snake BAC expressed the Hoxd11 to Hoxd4 genes in the developing limbs and genital bud.
source: the snake BAC expressed the Hoxd11 to Hoxd4 genes in the developing limbs and genital bud (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization data from snake BAC transgenic mice.

claim: While the mouse Hoxd9 to Hoxd3 genes were expressed at much higher levels in the trunk when compared to the genitals, the steady state levels of snake mRNAs were nearly the same in both tissues.
source: In such conditions, while the mouse Hoxd9 to Hoxd3 genes were expressed at much higher levels in the trunk when compared to the genitals, the steady state levels of snake mRNAs were nearly the same in both tissues (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on RT-qPCR data comparing mouse and snake genital and trunk tissues.

claim: The snake HoxD cluster lacks the sequences necessary to prevent Hox gene expression from the trunk lateral mesoderm.
source: Therefore, these results suggested that the snake HoxD cluster lacks the sequences necessary to prevent Hox gene expression from the trunk lateral mesoderm, a critical factor to properly develop limbs and genitals in mouse (see discussion).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on RT-qPCR and BAC transgenic data.

claim: Both the mouse Hoxd11 and Hoxd13 genes showed more interactions with the centromeric gene desert in the GT material than in control trunk material.
source: As expected, both the mouse Hoxd11 and Hoxd13 genes showed more interactions with the centromeric gene desert in the GT material than in control trunk material (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is based on 4C-seq data from mouse genital tubercle tissue.

claim: The snake Hoxd13 and Hoxd11 interaction profiles were not significantly different when either HP or the control samples were used.
source: In contrast, the snake Hoxd13 and Hoxd11 interaction profiles were not significantly different, when either HP or the control samples were used.
evidence: The claim is based on 4C-seq data from snake hemipenes tissue.

claim: The GT1 and GT2 sequences are well conserved in the snake.
source: We searched the snake gene desert for the presence of the GT1 and GT2 sequences, two DNA segments described in the mouse counterpart to specifically interact with Hoxd13 in the developing GT (Lonfat et al., 2014) (Figure 4C, bottom left) and could identify them (Figure 4C, bottom right).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The conserved GT1 and GT2 sequences in the snake did not significantly increase their interactions with Hoxd13 during the development of the snake genitals.
source: However, even though these sequences are well conserved in the snake, they did not significantly increase their interactions with Hoxd13 during the development of the snake genitals (Figure 4C, right).
evidence: The claim is based on 4C-seq data from snake hemipenes.

claim: Only the Prox sequence appeared to gain interactions in the snake HP sample when compared to control tissue.
source: In fact, the comparative analysis of the snake 4C-seq data revealed that, if anything, only the Prox sequence, a known mouse GT and limb enhancer (Gonzalez et al., 2007) appeared to gain interactions in the snake HP sample, when compared to control tissue.
evidence: The claim is based on 4C-seq data analysis.

claim: All mouse digit- and genital bud-specific enhancers conserved within mammals and up to birds showed some level of conservation in snakes.
source: Surprisingly, all these murine enhancers conserved within mammals and up to birds showed some level of conservation in snakes (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The mouse Prox sequence displayed activity in both the developing digits and GT.
source: The mouse counterpart of the Prox sequence displayed activity in both the developing digits and GT.
evidence: The claim is based on previous transgenic enhancer assays.

claim: The mouse GT2 sequence is a genital only-specific enhancer.
source: The mouse GT2 sequence is a genital only-specific enhancer
evidence: The claim is based on previous transgenic enhancer assays.

claim: The mouse Island I sequence displays limb-only enhancer specificity when placed upstream of a lacZ reporter in a transgenic assay.
source: the mouse Island I sequence displays limb-only enhancer specificity when placed upstream of a lacZ reporter in a transgenic assay (Montavon et al., 2011; Gonzalez et al., 2007; Lonfat et al., 2014) (Figure 5C, top).
evidence: The claim is based on previous transgenic enhancer assays.

claim: The snake Prox element elicited a robust lacZ staining in the developing mouse GT but staining was not detected in the growing limb buds.
source: The snake Prox element elicited a robust lacZ staining in the developing mouse GT. Interestingly however, and in contrast to the mouse sequence, staining was not detected in the growing limb buds, indicating that the snake Prox sequence had lost its potential to drive transcription in digits (Figure 5C, bottom).
evidence: The claim is based on transgenic enhancer assay data.

claim: The snake GT2 sequence was able to drive reporter gene expression in the mouse GT but the level of lacZ staining obtained was consistently weaker than with the mouse GT2 sequence.
source: Likewise, the snake GT2 sequence was able to drive reporter gene expression in the mouse GT. However, the level of lacZ staining obtained was consistently weaker than with the mouse GT2 sequence (Figure 5C, bottom)
evidence: The claim is based on transgenic enhancer assay data.

claim: The snake Island I was able to drive reporter gene expression in the mouse GT while unable to elicit any staining in the developing limb buds.
source: We then turned to the snake Island I, a mouse limb-specific enhancer sequence and, noteworthy, the snake version was able to drive reporter gene expression in the mouse GT while unable to elicit any staining in the developing limb buds (Figure 5C, top).
evidence: The claim is based on transgenic enhancer assay data.

claim: The chicken Island I construct elicited staining in limbs but not in the GT.
source: The chicken construct elicited staining in limbs but not in the GT, i.e. in a pattern reminiscent of the mouse rather than the snake Island I (Figure 5C, top).
evidence: The claim is based on transgenic enhancer assay data.

claim: The lizard Island I drove reporter gene expression in limbs and showed weak staining in the GT, displaying an intermediate enhancer specificity between the snakes and the other amniotes assayed.
source: Noteworthy, while the lizard Island I also drove reporter gene expression in limbs, weak staining was scored in the GT, somehow displaying an intermediate enhancer specificity between the snakes and the other amniotes assayed (Figure 5C, top).
evidence: The claim is based on transgenic enhancer assay data.

claim: Proper sequential Hox gene activation in time and space during the elongation of the main body axis is critical for the correct patterning of the axial skeleton.
source: Proper sequential Hox gene activation in time and space during the elongation of the main body axis is critical for the correct patterning of the axial skeleton (Deschamps and van Nes, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established knowledge.

claim: In tetrapods, regulatory elements controlling Hox gene expression are found at various positions.
source: In tetrapods, regulatory elements controlling Hox gene expression are found at various positions.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about Hox gene regulation.

claim: The mouse HoxD cluster contains regulatory elements which are mainly involved in driving Hox gene expression along the anterior-posterior body axis during gastrulation.
source: The mouse HoxD cluster for instance contains regulatory elements, which are mainly involved in driving Hox gene expression along the anterior-posterior body axis during gastrulation, whereas remote enhancers located outside of the cluster itself regulate transcription in other organs or structures (Spitz et al., 2001; Lonfat and Duboule, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Remote enhancers located outside of the mouse HoxD cluster regulate transcription in other organs or structures.
source: The mouse HoxD cluster for instance contains regulatory elements, which are mainly involved in driving Hox gene expression along the anterior-posterior body axis during gastrulation, whereas remote enhancers located outside of the cluster itself regulate transcription in other organs or structures (Spitz et al., 2001; Lonfat and Duboule, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In most vertebrates, regulatory sequences located in the gene deserts flanking the HoxD cluster are necessary for proper expression in the embryonic trunk mesoderm.
source: However, our various transgenic mouse lines containing HoxD clusters from different vertebrate species showed that, in most vertebrates, regulatory sequences located in the gene deserts flanking the HoxD cluster are necessary for proper expression in the embryonic trunk mesoderm.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the BAC transgenic experiments.

claim: In snakes, long-range mesodermal enhancers may have been progressively complemented by local enhancers to regulate Hoxd gene expression in the developing body axis.
source: In an evolutionary context, it is possible that in snakes, long-range mesodermal enhancers were progressively complemented by local enhancers to regulate Hoxd gene expression in the developing body axis, perhaps to provide an increased fine-tuned control in the expression balance between single Hoxd genes during embryonic development.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a possible evolutionary scenario.

claim: The snake HoxD cluster BAC was the only transgenic configuration where expression was strong in the limbs and external genitals.
source: It is however worth noting that the snake HoxD cluster BAC was the only transgenic configuration where expression was strong in the limbs and external genitals, whereas BACs derived from animals with limbs did not elicit an expression of Hoxd genes into the transgenic limbs, even though the endogenous genes were strongly expressed there.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of BAC transgenic expression patterns.

claim: In the absence of limbs, negative control preventing Hox gene expression from trunk lateral mesoderm may have been lost in the course of snake evolution.
source: Our results using the corn snake BAC suggest that, in the absence of limbs, this negative control may have been lost in the course of evolution, leading to the maintenance of transcription in all mesoderm derivatives.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the snake BAC transgenic data.

claim: Hox clusters of jawed vertebrates show high levels of chromatin compaction.
source: Hox clusters of jawed vertebrates show high levels of chromatin compaction (Noordermeer et al., 2011; Fabre et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Squamate Hox clusters have accumulated a large number of transposable elements.
source: Squamate Hox clusters however seem to slightly deviate from this rule by having accumulated a large number of transposable elements (Di-Poï et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The general bimodal TAD regulatory structure is conserved at the HoxD locus between mouse and snake.
source: However, a significant difference was scored in the interaction profiles of Hoxd9, which displayed more contacts further away of region CNS39 in the mouse than in the snake sample. As this regulatory region is particularly active in proximal limbs, the lower frequency of contacts observed in snake embryos was not unexpected. This observation indicates that, while the general bimodal TAD regulatory structure is conserved at the HoxD locus, differences between vertebrate species may exist either in the extent, or in the internal organization of interactions within the TADs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on 4C-seq data comparing mouse and snake.

claim: A significant overlap between limb and genital cis-regulatory mechanisms was recently reported.
source: However, tetrapod limb-specific enhancers are often conserved in snakes and a significant overlap between limb and genital cis-regulatory mechanisms was recently reported (Infante et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: When a mouse limb- and genital-specific Tbx4 enhancer sequence was isolated from snake, it could only recapitulate genital expression, having lost the limb-specific regulatory potential.
source: Indeed when a mouse limb- and genital-specific Tbx4 enhancer sequence was isolated from snake, it could only recapitulate genital expression, thus having lost the limb-specific regulatory potential (Infante et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The mouse Prox consists of two regulatory modules.
source: Consistent with this observation, we find that the snake counterpart of the mouse limb and genital enhancer Prox (Gonzalez et al., 2007) has lost its limb regulatory potential, while keeping a strong capacity to drive expression in the developing genitalia. This suggests that the mouse Prox consists of two regulatory modules, while the snake Prox has kept the genital specificity only.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the differential activity of mouse and snake Prox sequences.

claim: Island I had a limb-only activity at the time of divergence between mammals and reptiles/birds.
source: On the other hand, the chicken Island I revealed enhancer specificities almost identical to those of the mouse sequence despite the fact that birds are more closely related to squamates than to mammals, suggesting that Island I had a limb-only activity at the time of divergence between mammals and reptiles/birds.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparative enhancer activity data.

claim: The co-option of Island I to a genital function likely occurred in the squamate clade and preceded limb loss in snakes.
source: Interestingly, the lizard sequence displayed a weak activity in the genital bud, in addition to the limb, indicating that the co-option to a genital function likely occurred in the squamate clade and thus preceded limb loss in snakes.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the lizard Island I enhancer activity.

claim: External genitalia of squamates, unlike that of mammals, were proposed to have the same embryonic origin as limbs.
source: External genitalia of squamates, unlike that of mammals, were proposed to have the same embryonic origin as limbs (Tschopp et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: While the general bimodal regulatory strategy is conserved, some profound differences in the regulation are scored at the HoxD locus between mouse and snake.
source: Altogether our results show that, while the general bimodal regulatory strategy is conserved, some profound differences in the regulation are scored at the HoxD locus between two species displaying strikingly distinct morphologies.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: Vertebrates with extreme variations in systems known to be under the control of Hox genes rely upon the same general regulatory architecture and principles at Hox loci.
source: It nevertheless indicates that vertebrates with extreme variations in those systems known to be under the control of Hox genes (vertebral number and identities, limbs, genitals) rely upon the same general regulatory architecture and principles at Hox loci.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: Vertebrate morphological evolution was accompanied by changes in Hox gene regulation, yet such variations were constrained within the general regulatory framework found at these loci.
source: In this view, vertebrate morphological evolution was accompanied by changes in Hox gene regulation, yet such variations were constrained within the general regulatory framework found at these loci.
evidence: The claim is an inference and interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: A 1.3 Mb large DNA sequence of high quality was obtained from 13 overlapping BACs covering the corn snake HoxD locus.
source: A scaffold was built out of 13 overlapping BACs, which were selected for sequencing and from which a 1.3 Mb large DNA sequence of high quality was obtained (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on the sequencing and assembly work performed.

claim: All Hoxd genes in the corn snake share the same transcriptional orientation within the cluster.
source: The structural analysis of the corn snake HoxD cluster revealed that, as for other species of snakes whose genomes were recently released (Vonk et al., 2013; Castoe et al., 2013), all Hoxd genes but Hoxd12 are present and share the same transcriptional orientation within the cluster.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of the sequenced cluster.

claim: The increased size of the snake HoxD cluster is likely due to a higher repeat content.
source: When compared to the mouse, the corn snake cluster is about 1.5 fold larger (Figure 1A) (Vonk et al., 2013), likely due to a higher repeat content (Di-Poï et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is an inference based on repeat content analysis and cited literature.

claim: The pattern of conservation of the snake HoxD genomic landscape is almost identical to that of the chicken when compared to the mouse sequence.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the pattern of conservation of the snake HoxD genomic landscape is almost identical to that of the chicken, when compared to the mouse sequence (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on global conservation analysis.

claim: The proper collinear regulation of Hox gene transcription in tetrapods was associated with the progressive removal of H3K27me3 coverage.
source: In tetrapods, the proper collinear regulation of Hox gene transcription was associated with the progressive removal of H3K27me3 coverage (Soshnikova and Duboule, 2009), a histone modification deposited by the Polycomb complex PRC2 (Margueron and Reinberg, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The HoxD cluster is surrounded by two gene deserts of approximately 1 Mb in size in the mouse.
source: The HoxD cluster is surrounded by two gene deserts of approximately 1 Mb (megabase) in size, each one containing distinct sets of enhancers capable of activating specific sub-groups of target Hoxd genes depending on their location within the cluster.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about the mouse HoxD locus.

claim: Each of the two gene deserts flanking the mouse HoxD cluster can be superimposed to a Topologically Associating Domain (TAD).
source: Each of these two gene deserts can be superimposed to a Topologically Associating Domain (TAD), i.e. a chromatin domain where DNA-DNA interactions in cis are privileged, for example between promoters and enhancers, and determined through chromosome conformation capture technologies (Dixon et al., 2012; Nora et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The centromeric gene desert can activate the transcription of the Hoxd9 to Hoxd13 genes in the mouse.
source: The centromeric gene desert can activate the transcription of the Hoxd9 to Hoxd13 genes, whereas the telomeric gene desert, which is further subdivided into two sub-TADs (Andrey et al., 2013) controls the expression of Hoxd1 to Hoxd11 (see [Lonfat and Duboule, 2015]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The telomeric gene desert controls the expression of Hoxd1 to Hoxd11 in the mouse.
source: The centromeric gene desert can activate the transcription of the Hoxd9 to Hoxd13 genes, whereas the telomeric gene desert, which is further subdivided into two sub-TADs (Andrey et al., 2013) controls the expression of Hoxd1 to Hoxd11 (see [Lonfat and Duboule, 2015]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The telomeric TAD initially controls all genes from Hoxd3 to Hoxd11 in the proximal part of the mouse limb bud.
source: During limb development, for instance, the telomeric TAD initially controls all genes from Hoxd3 to Hoxd11 in the proximal part of the limb bud, whereas more posterior genes such as Hoxd13 or Hoxd12 are controlled subsequently in the most distal aspect of the incipient limb by enhancers located within the centromeric TAD (Andrey et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: More posterior genes such as Hoxd13 or Hoxd12 are controlled in the most distal aspect of the mouse limb by enhancers located within the centromeric TAD.
source: During limb development, for instance, the telomeric TAD initially controls all genes from Hoxd3 to Hoxd11 in the proximal part of the limb bud, whereas more posterior genes such as Hoxd13 or Hoxd12 are controlled subsequently in the most distal aspect of the incipient limb by enhancers located within the centromeric TAD (Andrey et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The centromeric TAD controls transcription of posterior Hoxd genes during the outgrowth of mouse external genitalia.
source: This latter regulatory landscape also controls transcription of the same posterior genes during the outgrowth of external genitalia (Lonfat et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Snakes display highly specialized and divergent external genitals.
source: Since snakes are limbless animals and they display highly specialized and divergent external genitals (Tschopp et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Snakes have a tetrapod-like complement of Hox genes with only a few exceptions.
source: These analyses revealed that snakes, regardless of their extreme morphologies, have a tetrapod-like complement of Hox genes with only a few exceptions (Vonk et al., 2013; Di-Poï et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous genomic analyses.

claim: The analysis of Hox gene expression in the developing corn snake revealed a surprisingly well conserved collinear mRNA distribution along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: The analysis of Hox gene expression in the developing corn snake (Pantherophis guttatus) revealed a surprisingly well conserved collinear mRNA distribution along the anterior-posterior axis.
evidence: The claim is based on previous expression analysis studies.

claim: The strict correlation between morphological landmarks and the anterior borders of Hox transcript domains seen in mammals and birds was not always present in snakes.
source: However, the rather strict correlation between morphological landmarks and the anterior borders of Hox transcript domains, usually seen in mammals and birds, was not always present in snakes (Burke et al., 1995; Woltering et al., 2009) (see also Head and Polly [2015]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Some Hox proteins in snakes had likely changed part of their functionality.
source: It was thus concluded that some Hox proteins had likely changed (part of) their functionality.
evidence: The claim is an inference from previous studies on Hox expression patterns.

claim: The most posterior Hox genes were poorly expressed in the extending tailbud of snakes.
source: In addition, the fact that the most posterior Hox genes were poorly expressed in the extending tailbud was tentatively associated to the unusually large number of segments (Di-Poï et al., 2010), together with an increased pace in segmentation (Gomez et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The extreme body plan observed in snakes is associated with an extensive regulatory restructuring at the HoxD locus.
source: We find that, even though the structural organization of the corn snake HoxD cluster resembles that of tetrapods, the extreme body plan observed in snakes is associated with an extensive regulatory restructuring.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference based on all the findings presented.

claim: In snakes, mesodermal enhancers are mostly located inside the cluster itself, whereas other vertebrates make use of long-range regulations located at remote positions.
source: In snakes, mesodermal enhancers are mostly located inside the cluster itself, whereas other vertebrates make use of long-range regulations located at remote positions.
evidence: The claim is a summary of findings from BAC transgenic and ChIP-seq experiments.

claim: Despite the loss of limbs, the bimodal chromatin organisation at the Hoxd locus found in tetrapods is conserved in the snake lineage.
source: In addition, we show that despite the loss of limbs, the bimodal chromatin organisation at the Hoxd locus found in tetrapods is conserved in the snake lineage.
evidence: The claim is based on 4C-seq data showing bimodal interaction patterns.

claim: The regulation of snake Hoxd genes during the development of the external genitalia is different from that of other tetrapods.
source: However, we find that the regulation of snake Hoxd genes during the development of the external genitalia is different from that of other tetrapods, even though the general logic is conserved.
evidence: The claim is based on 4C-seq and enhancer assay data.

claim: The change in enhancer activity from a limb to an external genital specificity seems to have occurred in the Island I sequence.
source: In this latter case, the change in enhancer activity from a limb to an external genital specificity seems to have occurred.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparative enhancer assay data.

claim: Hoxd gene regulation in the snake is in many ways distinct from the situation in mammals.
source: Altogether, we conclude that Hoxd gene regulation in the snake is in many ways distinct from the situation in mammals.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on all experimental findings.

claim: Vertebrate species can display different morphologies yet contain a strikingly similar repertoire of transcription factors and signalling molecules.
source: Even though vertebrate species can display different morphologies, they all contain a strikingly similar repertoire of transcription factors and signalling molecules.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge in evolutionary developmental biology.

claim: Genes with critical functions during embryonic development are often largely pleiotropic and highly conserved across species.
source: In particular, genes with critical functions during embryonic development are often largely pleiotropic and highly conserved across species (for references, see Kirschner et al., 2005; Duboule and Wilkins, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Hox genes and their structural and functional organization into genomic clusters were found well conserved across bilateria.
source: Initially, Hox genes, as well as their structural and functional organization into genomic clusters were found well conserved across bilateria (Duboule and Dolle, 1989; Akam, 1989; Garcia-Fernandez and Holland, 1994; Graham et al., 1989; McGinnis et al., 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to foundational work.

claim: Tetrapods generally have four clusters of Hox genes (HoxA, HoxB, HoxC and HoxD).
source: Tetrapods generally have four clusters of Hox genes (HoxA, HoxB, HoxC and HoxD), originating from genome duplications early in the vertebrate lineage (see e.g. Lemons and McGinnis, 2006)
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The four Hox clusters in tetrapods are located on different chromosomes.
source: Tetrapods generally have four clusters of Hox genes (HoxA, HoxB, HoxC and HoxD), originating from genome duplications early in the vertebrate lineage (see e.g. Lemons and McGinnis, 2006) and located on different chromosomes
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge.

claim: All vertebrate Hox clusters described thus far implement collinearity, whereby Hox genes are expressed sequentially in both time and space following their topological organization within each genomic cluster.
source: In addition, all vertebrate Hox clusters described thus far implement a particular type of regulatory process referred to as collinearity, whereby Hox genes are expressed sequentially in both time and space following their topological organization within each genomic cluster (Gaunt et al., 1988; Izpisua-Belmonte et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to foundational work.

claim: Collinearity is first observed during axial extension and subsequently in some structures such as the limbs.
source: This regulatory property is first observed during axial extension and, subsequently, in some structures such as the limbs (see (Deschamps, 2007; Deschamps and van Nes, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Collinearity in limbs was likely co-opted in the course of tetrapod evolution through the emergence of global enhancers located at remote positions on both sides of the cluster.
source: In this latter case, and while the detailed underlying mechanism may be distinct from that at work in the major body axis (Kmita and Duboule, 2003), the general principle remains the same and was likely co-opted in the course of tetrapod evolution (Spitz et al., 2001), through the emergence of global enhancers located at remote positions on both sides of the cluster (Lonfat et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.
